input.title: Database indexes
input.description: How B-tree indexes speed up reads and what they cost on writes.
input.projectGoal: Become comfortable designing schemas for a production Postgres app

output.title: Why indexes exist
output.bodyMarkdown:
### The problem indexes solve

Without an index, Postgres answers `WHERE email = $1` with a sequential scan: it reads every row in the table and discards the ones that do not match.

- On a 10-row table this is instant.
- On a 10-million-row table it is seconds of disk I/O per query.

### What an index actually is

A B-tree index is a separate, sorted structure that maps column values to row locations. Looking up a value walks the tree instead of scanning the table.

output.title: What indexes cost
output.bodyMarkdown:
### Writes get slower

Every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` must also update every index on the table.

1. A table with five indexes does six writes per insert, not one.
2. Indexes consume disk and memory that would otherwise cache table data.

### The practical rule

Index the columns you filter, join, and sort on. Then delete the indexes that `pg_stat_user_indexes` shows are never scanned.

output.title: Cache-Control decides who may store a response
output.bodyMarkdown:
### The directives that matter

`Cache-Control` is the response header that tells every cache between your server and the user what it may do.

- `max-age=60` — a browser may reuse this response for 60 seconds without asking.
- `s-maxage=600` — shared caches (CDNs) may reuse it for 10 minutes, overriding `max-age`.
- `private` — only the browser may store it, never a CDN.
- `no-store` — nobody may keep a copy.

### Choosing a value

Pick the longest duration where a stale response is still acceptable, then shorten it only when that turns out to be wrong.

output.title: ETags turn expiry into revalidation
output.bodyMarkdown:
### The conditional request

When a cached response expires, the client does not have to refetch the whole body.

1. The server sends `ETag: "abc123"` alongside the response.
2. On the next request the client sends `If-None-Match: "abc123"`.
3. If nothing changed, the server replies `304 Not Modified` with an empty body.

### Why this matters

A 304 still costs a round trip, but it saves the payload. For a large JSON document or an image, that is most of the cost.
